title: The Logbook

post.author: u/twelve_to_four_sigvaldi
post.title: I keep the night watch in a cargo ship's engine room. At 03:00 the power blinked, and by 03:07 she leaned 2 degrees to port. The controller's ledger says she's level.

blocks.text: I'm third engineer on the MV Brannock Petrel, a small cargo ship, and I keep the twelve-to-four watch in the engine room. Low in her hull sit two ballast tanks of seawater, port and starboard. The ballast controller keeps her upright by moving water between them in 9 steps: open valves 1 to 4, run the transfer pump, close valves 4 to 1. Benedikta, our electro-technical officer, fitted it last year. After each step it writes a line in its ledger, a file on a memory card.
On Tuesday the fuel burn had left her 2 degrees to starboard: 250 tonnes in the starboard tank, 150 in port. At 02:54:40 I started a trim to move 50 tonnes across. The controller's screen:

02:54:40  step 1  valve 1 open
02:55:00  step 2  valve 2 open
02:55:10  ledger saved to card: steps 1-2
02:55:20  step 3  valve 3 open
02:55:40  step 4  valve 4 open
02:56:00  step 5  transfer pump on, 4 min, 50 t
03:00:00  step 5  pump off
03:00:00  POWER BLIP
03:00:40  rebooted. ledger: steps 1-2 done. resuming at step 3
03:01:40  step 5  transfer pump on, 4 min, 50 t
03:07:00  step 9  valve 1 closed. trim done. ledger list 0.0
While it rebooted I went down with a torch. Valves 3 and 4 were open, both of them. The ledger says they never were. I was still on the ladder when the pump started again.
Somewhere aft, a pencil began to roll, and didn't stop.

By 03:07 the inclinometer read 2 degrees to port. Mugs crept along the mess table, and a chair slid until the wall stopped it. On the chief's old desk the paper engine-room logbook, unused since the controller came, lay open. In pencil, in a hand nobody aboard writes, were three lines the ledger doesn't have: V3 OPEN 02:55:20. V4 OPEN 02:55:40. PUMP 4 MIN 02:56:00. Above the desk, on the bulkhead:

blocks.title: PAINTED ON THE ENGINE ROOM BULKHEAD
items: WRITE IT IN THE LOGBOOK BEFORE YOU DO IT.

blocks.text: Benedikta says the paint is about paper logbooks and the ledger is software. She wants the controller fixed before tonight's trim. What should she change?

blocks.label: controller_tuesday_030700.png

diagram.aria: Benedikta's drawing of 03:07:00 on Tuesday. The ballast controller has finished the trim; it writes its ledger after each step. The ledger on the memory card lists steps 1 to 9, each once, and so says the ship is level. The inclinometer reads 2.0 degrees to port. The port tank holds 250 tonnes and the starboard tank 150, where the trim planned 200 each: the pump moved 100 tonnes for a 50 tonne trim.

notes.text: moved 100 t for a 50 t trim

blocks.caption: Benedikta's drawing of 03:07:00 on Tuesday. The ledger lists every step once, so by its own count the trim moved 50 tonnes and she is level. The tanks say the pump moved 100: port 250 tonnes, starboard 150, and the inclinometer reads 2.0 degrees to port.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two records disagree, and the water settles it. Some words first. When a program writes to a file, the bytes usually land in a cache in memory, and the system saves them to the disk or card later; fsync is the call that says save it now, and don't come back until it's saved. A database numbers every record in its log in order, a log sequence number, LSN for short, so it can always tell which came first. And a checkpoint, in a database, is a moment when it makes sure everything up to some record has reached its data files, and writes down which record that was. Now your screen. At 03:00:00, which of the ledger's lines existed only in memory? If every line had been saved the instant it was written, would step 5's line have made it? When the controller came back, what could it have looked at, besides its own ledger, to learn what had already happened? And read the pump's step out loud: if the controller did it twice, what would happen twice?

replies.author: u/twelve_to_four_sigvaldi
replies.text: Benedikta says the card saves new lines every five minutes, at 02:55:10, 03:00:10 and so on, to spare it wear, so it last saved at 02:55:10. She also says every valve, and the tank gauge, has a small memory of its own, a plate that keeps the last command number it was given. The controller has never sent them one.

comments.author: u/every_second_peregrine
comments.text: You lost five minutes of ledger because you saved every five minutes. That's the whole bug. Our sorting-line controllers save their ledger every second, a checkpoint every second with fsync, and in six years we've never lost more than a second. What's to lose in one second? Change one number in the config file and go back to bed. Leave the old chief's paint to the old chief.

comments.author: u/run_it_back_florentyna
comments.text: Your bulkhead is right, and it's what databases do: write it down first. Log 'open valve 3' and 'run the pump 4 minutes', save it, then do it. After any reboot, replay the whole log from the top, so nothing that was logged can ever be missed. We run the dosing pumps at our water plant that way.

comments.author: u/belt_and_braces_marguerite
comments.text: Everyone here is rewriting software for a power problem. A blip rebooted the controller, so stop the blips: put it on an uninterruptible power supply, a UPS, a battery that takes over the instant the mains dips. Ours carries our control room for 10 minutes. Nothing has rebooted in a year.

reply.prompt: Tonight's trim starts at 02:54:40 again. What should Benedikta change in the controller? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep writing the ledger after each step, but force every line to the card at once instead of every five minutes.
options.verdict: A smaller gap, still a gap
options.part2: Benedikta made the controller fsync every ledger line the moment it's written, no more five-minute wait. Tonight I started the trim at 02:54:40. At 03:00:00 the pump stopped, and in the same second the lights blinked. The controller was back at 03:00:40 and read its ledger: steps 1 to 4, every line saved. Not one lost. Step 5 wasn't there, because the pump had stopped and the power went before the controller could write that it had. So at 03:01:00 it ran the pump again, 4 minutes, another 50 tonnes. At 03:06:20 the trim was done, the ledger said level, and the inclinometer said 2 degrees to port. The pencil rolled off the console. I didn't pick it up.
options.senior: Saving more often shrinks the window but can't close it. As long as the controller acts first and writes it down after, there's a moment when a step is done and unrecorded, and a restart that trusts the ledger does it again. Here the gap went from five minutes to one step, and the step was the pump. Write the record first, force it to disk before acting, and make it safe to apply twice.

options.text: Before each step, log its end state and number and fsync it; on boot, from the last checkpoint, redo what plates lack.
options.part2: Benedikta rewrote it the way the bulkhead says. Before each step the controller writes the state the step will leave, with the next number, No. 4119 for 'valve 3: open', No. 4121 for 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t', forces it to the card, and only then acts. When a step is done it writes that number on the device's plate, and every 3 records it checks the valves and writes a checkpoint. Tonight the lights blinked at 03:00:00 again, the second the pump stopped. At 03:00:40 the controller came back, read from its last checkpoint, after No. 4119, and checked two records: No. 4120, valve 4 open, and No. 4121, the tanks at 200 and 200. Both plates already showed them, so it did neither again. At 03:01:00 it closed valve 4, and at 03:02:00 the trim was done. Level. Nothing slid. In the morning the paper logbook was open on the chief's desk at a fresh page, with one line in pencil: WELL KEPT.
options.senior: That's write-ahead logging done whole. The record reaches the card before the change it describes, so nothing can have happened that the log doesn't know about. Each record carries a sequence number and says how things should end up, so recovery can compare it with the plate and apply only what's missing; applying a state twice is harmless, which running a pump twice is not. Checkpoints keep recovery short. Databases do exactly this, with pages instead of valves.

options.text: Write each step to the log before doing it, as the bulkhead says, force it to the card, and replay the whole log on boot.
options.verdict: First is right, the replay isn't
options.part2: Benedikta did as Florentyna said. Before each step the controller writes the step, 'open valve 3', 'run the transfer pump 4 min', forces it to the card, then does it, and on every boot it replays the whole log from the top. Tonight the lights blinked at 03:00:00, the second the pump stopped. The log was all there this time, No. 4117 to 4121, the pump included. At 03:00:40 the controller replayed all five. The valves were already open, so that changed nothing. The pump record said run 4 minutes, so it ran 4 minutes, 03:00:40 to 03:04:40, and 50 more tonnes went to port. At 03:06:00 the trim was done, the log said level, and the inclinometer said 2 degrees to port. The log was right about everything it had been told. It just said it twice.
options.senior: Logging first fixes half of it: nothing can happen that the log doesn't know about. But replay has to be safe to repeat, and 'run the pump 4 minutes' isn't: replaying it moves the water again. A record should say what the result is, 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t', with a sequence number, so recovery can see from the plate that it already happened and skip it. And replaying from the top grows with the log: a checkpoint lets recovery start near the end.

options.text: Put the controller on a battery, so a blip like Tuesday's at 03:00 can never reboot it in the middle of a trim again.
options.verdict: Trade-off: fewer crashes, not safe ones
options.part2: Benedikta put the controller on a UPS that carries it for 10 minutes. Tonight the lights blinked at 03:00:00 and the controller never noticed: the trim was done at 03:01:20, level. Two weeks later, at 03:00:00 on the dot, the second the pump stopped, the controller froze on a software fault nobody has found yet, and its watchdog restarted it. The battery was full. Steps 3 and 4 were still waiting for the card, and step 5 had never been written. It was back at 03:00:40, said steps 1-2 done, and ran the pump again from 03:01:40. At 03:07:00 she lay 2 degrees to port. The ledger says level.
options.senior: A battery is worth having: fewer blips means fewer crashes. But power is only one way to stop a program in the middle. A bug, a watchdog restart, a dead battery or a pulled card will all do it, and the controller still acts first and records after, saving every five minutes. Make recovery correct after any crash, and keep the battery as a way to have fewer of them.

sim.title: Run the ballast trim on the Brannock Petrel
sim.lede: You're Benedikta, replaying one trim. The tanks start at port 150 t and starboard 250 t, and the sim counts only the tanks: the list is (starboard tonnes minus port tonnes) divided by 50, in degrees, so she starts 2.0 degrees to starboard. The trim has 9 steps from 02:54:40: open valves 1 to 4, run the transfer pump (4 minutes at 12.5 t a minute, 50 t), close valves 4 to 1. Each step starts 20 s after the last one finishes, and valve steps take no time. Ledger after each step: the controller acts, then writes a line. Log actions first: it writes 'run the transfer pump 4 min' before acting, and on boot replays every record after the last checkpoint, or the whole log without one. Log states and numbers first: it writes the end state, such as 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t', numbered from No. 4117 (each trim gets a new log file, and the numbers carry on from the last trim's No. 4116); when a step is done it sets that device's plate; on boot it applies a record only if the plate shows a lower number, and pumps only until the tanks read the record. With fsync off a line waits for the card's five-minute save at 02:55:10, 03:00:10 and 03:05:10; with fsync on it's on the card at once. A blip comes after any step that finishes in that second and before any line due in it, and the controller is back 40 s later. A checkpoint, in the two logs-first modes, checks every valve and the tanks after every 2 or 3 records and writes a line saying everything up to that number is done. Changing a setting replays the trim, and the clock runs ten times as fast as real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to the end as Tuesday. Steps 3 and 4 are lost from memory, step 5 was never written, the pump runs again from 03:01:40, and at 03:07:00 the log says level while she lists 2.0 degrees to port. Turn fsync on: nothing lost, but the pump still runs again, from 03:01:00. Pick the blip at 02:58:00: 75 t moved, 1.0 degrees to port. Back at 03:00:00, log actions first: 5 records replayed, and the pump repeats. Now log states and numbers: 5 records checked, none applied, level at 03:02:00. Set checkpoints to every 3 records, then every 2: 2 records checked, then 1. Try 02:58:00 again: one record applied, and the pump runs only 2 minutes. Last, turn fsync off: 3 records written and lost, and 3 plates ahead of the log.

explain.oneLine: Nothing aboard the Petrel moved the water. The controller acted first and wrote its ledger after, its lines waited five minutes for the card, and on reboot it believed the ledger: steps 3 to 5 had never happened, so it ran the pump twice.

steps.title: Do, then write it down: a gap that never closes.
steps.text: The controller acted first and wrote the ledger after, and its lines waited in memory until the card's five-minute save. At 03:00:00 two lines, steps 3 and 4, were still waiting, so the blip wiped them, and step 5's line hadn't been written at all: the pump stopped and the power went in the same second. On reboot the controller trusted its ledger, which said only steps 1 and 2 had happened. Opening valves 3 and 4 again was harmless, because they were already open. Running the pump again was not: 50 more tonnes went to port, and the ledger, with every step once, still said level. Saving every line at once with fsync, as Peregrine suggests, shrinks the gap to one step but can't close it. While the record comes after the act, there is always a moment when the act is done and unrecorded, and in the sim that moment fell on the pump.

steps.title: Write-ahead: the record goes first, and reaches the disk first.
steps.text: A database keeps a log beside its data files. PostgreSQL's manual puts the central concept like this: changes to data files must be written only after those changes have been logged, that is, after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. That's write-ahead logging, the WAL a standby replays in the reading-room case, and it's the chief's paint: write it in the logbook before you do it. A commit only has to force the log to disk, not every page it changed. The log is written in order, end after end, which is much cheaper than writing pages all over the disk, and one fsync can commit many transactions at once. After a crash, any change the data files missed is redone from the log, which PostgreSQL calls roll-forward recovery, or REDO. With the record first, nothing can have happened that the log doesn't know about.

steps.title: Records must be safe to apply twice.
steps.text: Logging first isn't enough if replay repeats an action. 'Run the pump 4 minutes' is an action record: replayed after the pump already ran, it moves the water twice, which is what Florentyna's plan would do. So a database writes state records instead: each says what the result is, such as the new contents of a page, and carries its LSN. Each data page remembers the LSN of the last record applied to it: PostgreSQL's page header has a field, pd_lsn, that tracks the most recent WAL entry related to the page. On recovery a record is applied only if the page hasn't seen it, that is, only if the record's LSN is higher than the page's. Applying 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t' to tanks that already read that changes nothing, and comparing numbers shows it already happened. Those are the plates on the Petrel's valves. A pump run is not a page write, which is why the fix logs where the tanks should end up, not how long to pump.

steps.title: Checkpoints: where recovery starts.
steps.text: Without checkpoints, recovery would read the log from its very first record. A checkpoint flushes every dirty page, a page changed in memory but not yet written to its data file, and then writes a checkpoint record, so nothing earlier is needed to recover from a crash. PostgreSQL's crash recovery looks at the latest checkpoint record to find the point in the WAL where it should start redoing. It begins a checkpoint every checkpoint_timeout, 5 minutes by default, or sooner if max_wal_size, 1 GB by default, is about to be exceeded. On the Petrel a checkpoint every 3 records cut Tuesday's recovery from 5 records to 2. The cost is extra writing: each checkpoint flushes pages, and with full_page_writes on, the default, the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs the whole page.

steps.title: What you may turn off, and what you mustn't.
steps.text: PostgreSQL lets you trade a little durability for speed with synchronous_commit = off. COMMIT returns before its WAL is on disk, so a crash can lose the last few commits, at most three times wal_writer_delay, 200 ms by default, after success was reported. The manual calls that data loss, not data corruption: whatever log did reach the disk is replayed in commit order, so the database is as if those transactions had been aborted cleanly. Turning fsync off is different. PostgreSQL stops making sure the log reaches the disk before the pages it describes, and the manual warns of unrecoverable data corruption after a power failure or system crash; that's the plates ahead of the log in the sim. MySQL's InnoDB does the same job with its redo log, replayed while the server starts, before connections are accepted, and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, whose default of 1 flushes the log at every commit. And the other half of atomicity: a transaction whose commit record never reached the log is treated on recovery as aborted, its changes undone or ignored.

diagram.aria: Tonight, with the fix. Before the pump runs, the controller writes record No. 4121, port 200 tonnes and starboard 200 tonnes, to the memory card and forces it there with fsync. Then it pumps until the tanks read 200 and 200, and the tank gauge's plate gets No. 4121. At 03:00:00 the power blinks, and the controller is back at 03:00:40. It reads the log from its last checkpoint, after No. 4119, and asks whether Nos. 4120 and 4121 are already on the plates. Both are, so it skips both and finishes the trim level at 03:02:00.

explain.caption: Tonight, with the fix. Record No. 4121 says how the tanks should end up, and it's on the card before the pump starts. When the pump stops, the tank gauge's plate gets 4121. After the 03:00:00 blip the controller reads from its last checkpoint, after No. 4119, finds both later records already on the plates, skips them, and finishes at 03:02:00, level.

fix.title: The fix: log the end state first, number it, force it to the card, and replay only what's missing
fix.text: Before every step the controller writes a record of the state it's about to create, 'valve 3: open' or 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t', with the next number, and forces it to the card with fsync before it touches anything. When a step is done it writes that number on the device's plate. Every 3 records it checks every valve and the tanks and writes a checkpoint. On boot it reads from the last checkpoint and applies a record only where the plate shows a lower number, pumping only until the tanks read what the record says. Keep the UPS too: it means fewer crashes, though not safe ones. In a database the same fix is already built in: leave fsync on, and let the WAL, page LSNs and checkpoints do their work.

limits: The log protects what recovery can compare against a record. Anything the system does to the outside world, an email, a payment to another bank, a message to another service, has no plate to check: make each of those safe to repeat with its own key, which Season 4 covers.

fsync is only as honest as the disk. PostgreSQL's manual warns that drives which report a write as done while it's still only in their own cache can subvert the WAL, and a power failure might then lead to irrecoverable data corruption.

Durability isn't a backup. The log survives a crash of this machine, not a lost disk, a fire, or a mistaken DELETE, which it records faithfully. You still need backups kept somewhere else, and restores you have tested.

Tuesday: steps 3 and 4 lost, step 5 never written, the pump ran twice: 2.0 degrees to port.

Log states with numbers first, fsync on

explain.seniorTake: Any system that does something and then records that it did it has a gap, and a restart that trusts the record will redo whatever fell into it. Close the gap the way databases do: write the intent to a log first, force it to disk before acting, and make every record safe to apply twice by saying what the result should be and numbering it, so recovery can compare and skip what's already done. Checkpoints keep recovery short. Know what each setting trades: synchronous_commit = off risks the last few commits and nothing else, while fsync = off risks the whole database. And remember what the log doesn't cover: the pump, the email or the payment outside the database, and the disk itself. It is not a backup.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: Write-Ahead Logging
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's manual calls write-ahead logging a standard method for ensuring data integrity. Its central concept is that changes to data files, where tables and indexes reside, must be written only after those changes have been logged, after WAL records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. Then data pages don't need flushing on every commit, because after a crash any changes not yet applied to the data pages can be redone from the WAL records: roll-forward recovery, also known as REDO. Only the WAL file needs to be flushed to guarantee a commit, it is written sequentially, so syncing it costs much less than flushing data pages, and one fsync of the WAL file may suffice to commit many transactions.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: LSNs and where recovery starts
realWorld.text: The WAL internals page says the insert position is described by a Log Sequence Number (LSN), a byte offset into the WAL that increases monotonically with each new record, and that LSNs are used to measure the progress of replication and recovery. After a checkpoint its position is saved in the file pg_control, so at the start of recovery the server reads pg_control, then the checkpoint record, then performs the REDO operation by scanning forward from the WAL location the checkpoint record names. The same page warns that WAL can be subverted by disk drives that falsely report a successful write when they have only cached the data, and that a power failure then might lead to irrecoverable data corruption.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: every page carries an LSN
realWorld.text: In PostgreSQL's page layout, the first field of every page header, pd_lsn, tracks the most recent WAL entry related to the page: the next byte after the last byte of the WAL record for the last change to it. That number is what lets recovery tell whether a page has already seen a record.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: checkpoints
realWorld.text: Checkpoints, the manual says, are points in the sequence of transactions at which it is guaranteed that the heap and index data files have been updated with all information written before that checkpoint. At checkpoint time all dirty data pages are flushed to disk and a special checkpoint record is written to the WAL. In a crash, recovery looks at the latest checkpoint record to find the point in the WAL, the redo record, from which to start REDO. A checkpoint begins every checkpoint_timeout seconds, or if max_wal_size is about to be exceeded, whichever comes first; the defaults are 5 minutes and 1 GB. With full_page_writes set, as it is by default, the first change to a data page after each checkpoint logs the entire page.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: fsync and synchronous_commit
realWorld.text: With fsync on, the server tries to make sure updates are physically written to disk, which ensures the database cluster can recover to a consistent state after an operating system or hardware crash. Turning it off is often a performance benefit, but this can result in unrecoverable data corruption in the event of a power failure or system crash, so the manual advises it only if you can easily recreate your entire database from external data. synchronous_commit is on by default. In off mode a crash might lose some recent allegedly-committed transactions, with a maximum delay of three times wal_writer_delay, whose default is 200 milliseconds, but unlike fsync it does not create any risk of database inconsistency: the state is as if those transactions had been aborted cleanly.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: asynchronous commit
realWorld.text: Asynchronous commit lets transactions complete more quickly, at the cost that the most recent transactions may be lost if the database should crash. The manual stresses that the risk is data loss, not data corruption: the net effect is the loss of the last few transactions, and because transactions are replayed in commit order, no inconsistency can be introduced. fsync = off is different: it disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, so a hardware or operating system crash could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state.

realWorld.title: MySQL 8.4: InnoDB's redo log
realWorld.text: MySQL's manual describes the redo log as a disk-based data structure used during crash recovery to correct data written by incomplete transactions. The passage of data through the redo log files is represented by an ever-increasing LSN value, and modifications that did not finish updating data files before an unexpected shutdown are replayed automatically during initialization and before connections are accepted.

realWorld.title: MySQL 8.4: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit
realWorld.text: This setting controls the balance between strict ACID compliance for commit operations and higher performance. Its default of 1 is required for full ACID compliance: logs are written and flushed to disk at each transaction commit. With 0, logs are written and flushed to disk once per second; with 2, they are written after each commit and flushed once per second. In both cases, the manual says, transactions for which logs have not been flushed can be lost in a crash.

realWorld.title: ARIES, 1992
realWorld.text: C. Mohan, with D. Haderle, B. Lindsay, H. Pirahesh and P. Schwarz, described ARIES in the March 1992 issue of ACM Transactions on Database Systems: a recovery method using write-ahead logging. Its summary says ARIES uses a log sequence number in each page to correlate the state of a page with respect to logged updates of that page, and introduces the paradigm of repeating history: redo all missing updates before rolling back the loser transactions during restart after a system failure. Most databases' recovery today follows the same shape.

asked: How does a database survive a crash in the middle of a transaction?
What does fsync have to do with durability?
interview.answer: A database keeps a write-ahead log: before it changes a data page, it appends a record describing the change, and before it reports a commit, it forces the log up to that commit's record to disk with fsync. The pages themselves can stay in memory and reach disk later. After a crash it starts from the last checkpoint, the point up to which every dirty page was flushed, and replays the log forward. Each record has a log sequence number and each page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it, so a record is applied only if the page hasn't seen it; records describe the resulting change, which makes replay safe to repeat. Transactions with no commit record in the log are rolled back or treated as aborted, so you get atomicity, and every acknowledged commit is in the log on disk, so you get durability. fsync matters because a write normally only reaches the operating system's cache; without forcing it, a power cut can lose a log record the database already called committed, or let a page reach disk before its log record. That's why fsync off can corrupt a PostgreSQL database, while synchronous_commit off only risks the last few commits. MySQL's InnoDB does the same with its redo log and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1. And I'd add that durability isn't a backup: you still need copies elsewhere and tested restores.

A tank in the hull that holds ballast water. The Petrel has a port tank and a starboard tank.
How far a ship leans to one side, in degrees. In the sim, every 50 tonnes more on one side leans the Petrel 1 degree that way.
To move weight, here ballast water, so the ship floats level. Tuesday's trim was to move 50 tonnes from starboard to port.
Fuel used up during a voyage. Fuel tanks emptying unevenly can make a ship lean, which ballast then corrects.
An instrument that measures how far a ship leans, in degrees. It shows the real list, whatever any record says.
The Petrel's computer that runs a trim: it opens valves, runs the transfer pump and closes the valves, in 9 steps, and keeps a record of them.
The pump that moves ballast water from the starboard tank to the port tank: 12.5 tonnes a minute, so 4 minutes moves 50 tonnes.
The instrument that measures how much water a tank holds. On the Petrel it reads both tanks and has its own plate.
The officer who looks after a ship's electrical and control systems. Benedikta fitted the Petrel's ballast controller.
The ballast controller's record of the steps it has done, one line each, kept in a file on its memory card.
A small flash card that keeps data with the power off. Each write wears it a little, which is why the controller saved only every five minutes.
A power cut so short the lights only blink, but long enough to make a computer without a battery restart.
Restarting a computer. Everything it held only in memory, such as lines not yet saved, is gone.
The paper book engineers once wrote every action in, by hand. The Petrel's has been unused since the controller came.
The head of a ship's engineering department. E. Thwaite, who painted the bulkhead in 1971, was one.
A small memory on each valve and on the tank gauge that keeps the number of the last record applied to it, like a database page's LSN.
A system call that tells the operating system to save a file's cached writes to the disk now, and not return until they are saved. Also a PostgreSQL setting.
One entry in a database's log, describing one change. Each has a log sequence number.
The number a database gives each log record, always rising, so it can tell which came first. In PostgreSQL it's a byte position in the WAL.
A moment when a database makes sure every change up to some log record has reached its data files and records which one. Recovery starts there.
Another name for a configuration file: the settings a program reads when it starts.
A row of conveyors and machines that sorts parcels or goods, run by controllers like the Petrel's.
A pump that adds a measured amount of a chemical, such as chlorine, to water. Running one twice adds twice the dose.
The main electricity supply, from the ship's generators or the grid.
Uninterruptible power supply: a battery that takes over the instant the mains dips, so the equipment on it doesn't lose power.
A timer that restarts a computer if its software stops checking in, for example after it freezes.
Writing a record of each change to a log, and forcing it to disk, before changing the data itself. Recovery replays the log. Rule 1.
A file where a database keeps its tables and indexes, as pages. The log is kept separately.
Storage that keeps data when the power is off, such as a disk or a memory card.
To write data waiting in memory out to the disk, so a crash can't lose it.
Recovering after a crash by reading the log forward from a checkpoint and redoing every change the data files are missing.
Written one piece after another at the end of a file, as a log is. Much cheaper than writes scattered across the disk.
A position in a file counted in bytes from its start. A PostgreSQL LSN is a byte offset into the WAL.
A command that prints a setting's current value, such as SHOW fsync;.
The SQL statement that removes rows from a table. A mistaken one is logged and made durable like any other change.
A log record that says what to do, such as 'run the pump 4 minutes'. Replaying it after it already happened does it again.
A log record that says how things should end up, such as 'port 200 t, starboard 200 t'. Applying it twice leaves the same result.
The first few bytes of a database page, holding facts about the page itself, such as its LSN.
The field in a PostgreSQL page header that tracks the most recent WAL record that changed the page.
A page changed in memory but not yet written to its data file. A crash loses it, and recovery rebuilds it from the log.
The log record a database writes at a checkpoint, saying where in the log recovery should start.
A small PostgreSQL file that holds, among other things, the position of the latest checkpoint, so recovery knows where to begin.
The PostgreSQL setting for how often a checkpoint starts. The default is 5 minutes.
A PostgreSQL setting: when the WAL since the last checkpoint is about to grow past it, a checkpoint starts early. The default is 1 GB.
A PostgreSQL setting, on by default: the first change to a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page, so a half-written page can be repaired.
PostgreSQL's name for a table's main data file, as against its indexes.
A PostgreSQL setting, on by default. Off, COMMIT returns before its WAL is on disk: a crash may lose the last few commits, but not corrupt anything.
Reporting a commit as done before its log record is on disk. Faster, and a crash can lose the last few commits.
How often a PostgreSQL background process flushes WAL that hasn't been written yet. The default is 200 milliseconds.
Data left wrong or inconsistent, such as a page holding changes its log never recorded. Worse than losing the last few changes: you can't trust any of it.
The log record that marks a transaction as committed. A transaction with no commit record in the log is treated as aborted on recovery.
Cancelled: none of its changes count. On recovery they are undone or ignored.
Reversing the changes of a transaction that never committed, as part of recovery or a rollback.
InnoDB's write-ahead log: a structure on disk used during crash recovery to redo changes the data files are missing.
A MySQL setting. The default, 1, writes and flushes the redo log at every commit; 0 and 2 flush once a second and can lose commits in a crash.
Keeping all four ACID promises, including durability: a committed change survives a crash.
PostgreSQL's name for all the databases one server manages, stored in one data directory.
Memory inside a disk drive where writes wait. A drive that reports a write as done while it's only in this cache can defeat fsync.
A recovery method using write-ahead logging, published by C. Mohan and colleagues at IBM in 1992. It puts an LSN in each page.
A research journal on databases, published by the Association for Computing Machinery. ARIES appeared in it in March 1992.
ARIES's idea: on restart, first redo every missing change, then roll back the transactions that never committed.
In ARIES, a transaction that hadn't committed when the system failed, so recovery rolls it back.
Write it in the logbook before you do it. Never after. Write the record of a change, and force it to disk, before making the change.
The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control that expects backup copies of information, software and systems to be kept and regularly tested under an agreed policy.

atWork: Look for 'do, then record' in your own systems. A job runner that marks a job done after running it, a queue consumer that acknowledges a message after handling it, a payment service that calls the bank and then saves the result: each has the Petrel's gap, and a crash in it means the work runs again on restart. For each one, ask three things. Is the record written before or after the act, and does it reach disk, as a committed transaction or an fsync, before anything outside happens? If the work runs twice, is it safe: does the record say what the result should be, or carry a key or number the other side checks? And on restart, does the code compare before it redoes anything? Then check your databases' settings: PostgreSQL's fsync, synchronous_commit and checkpoint_timeout (SHOW fsync; shows one), or MySQL's innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit. If any of them trades durability for speed, find out who chose it and whether that data could be rebuilt. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.13 (information backup) expects backup copies of information, software and systems to be kept and regularly tested against an agreed backup policy. A write-ahead log and fsync give durability, surviving a crash of one machine; they are not backups, and an auditor will ask for tested restores as well, so build both in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's job runner picks a job, runs it, then sets status = 'done' in the database. One job emails each customer their monthly statement. After a server crashed in the middle of that job, 312 customers got two statements. Why, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The crash fell between doing the work and recording it, so the restart ran it again
Record the intent first, durably, before acting
Make each step safe to repeat: a per-customer record or key, checked before sending

recall.model: The job did the work first and recorded it after, so the crash landed in the gap: the emails had gone out, but status still said not done, so the restart ran it again and sent them twice. Close the gap the write-ahead way: record what you're about to do, committed to disk, before acting, and make each step safe to repeat. Give each statement an id, record 'statement 2026-10 for customer 88 sent' per customer, or use the email provider's idempotency key, and on restart skip any customer whose record already shows it. Marking done sooner or more often only shrinks the gap.

recall.prompt: To speed up commits, which PostgreSQL change can lose the last few committed transactions in a crash but won't corrupt the database?
recall.why: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT returns before its WAL is on disk, so a crash can lose the last few commits, at most three times wal_writer_delay; the manual says the risk is data loss, not data corruption. fsync = off stops PostgreSQL making sure the log reaches disk before the pages it describes, and the manual warns of unrecoverable corruption. A smaller max_wal_size only makes checkpoints more frequent.

recall.prompt: A wallet service writes each change to its log as 'add 10.00 to wallet 7' before applying it, and after any restart replays the log from the beginning. After a crash, some wallets show the same top-up twice, and restarts now take 20 minutes. What's wrong, and how would you fix both problems?

keyIdeas.idea: Replaying an action repeats it: each record should say the resulting state, so it's safe to apply twice
Number each record and apply it only if it's newer than what the row already has
Take checkpoints so recovery starts near the end of the log, not the beginning

recall.model: Logging first was right, but the records describe actions, and replaying 'add 10.00' after it was already applied adds it again. Make each record say the resulting state, 'wallet 7 balance = 60.00', and give it a sequence number; keep on each wallet row the number of the last record applied, and on recovery apply a record only if it's newer than that. Then a record is safe to apply twice, and records already applied are skipped. Take checkpoints: every so often make sure everything up to some record is in the table and note that number, so recovery starts from the last checkpoint instead of the beginning of the log.

recall.prompt: What does a checkpoint change about crash recovery?
options: Commits become durable without an fsync
The write-ahead log is no longer needed
Recovery can start at the checkpoint instead of the start of the log
A backup copy of the database is saved to another disk
recall.why: At a checkpoint every dirty page is flushed and a checkpoint record is written, so every change before it is already in the data files. Recovery reads the latest checkpoint record and redoes only from there. Commits still need the log forced to disk, and a checkpoint is not a backup: it lives on the same disk as everything else.

recall.prompt: A database recovering from a crash reaches a log record numbered 4120 for a page whose LSN is 4122. What does it do with the record?
options: Applies it again, to be safe
Skips it: the page already holds a later change
Stops recovery, because the page is corrupt
Resets the page to the record's contents, then replays 4121 and 4122
recall.why: The page's LSN says the last record applied to it was 4122, so it has already seen 4120 and everything up to 4122. Applying 4120 again could undo the later changes, so recovery skips it. That comparison is what makes replay safe to repeat, like the plates on the Petrel's valves.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The trim controller has been perfect: every record numbered, forced to the card, checked against the plates. Then the cargo office's new booking database, PostgreSQL on a server in the ship's office, got slow at month-end, and a contractor set fsync = off, saying the write-ahead log already makes it crash-safe. Last night a power cut took the office down. This morning PostgreSQL keeps stopping, and one table shows two different rows for the same booking. Benedikta says the WAL was right there on the disk the whole time.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and what should Benedikta do now and next time?

keyIdeas.idea: With fsync off the log isn't forced to disk before the pages it describes, so a power cut leaves them in any order: corruption, not just loss
Don't trust the damaged files: restore from a backup and replay archived WAL, or rebuild
Leave fsync on; for speed use synchronous_commit = off, which risks only the last few commits

coldCase.model: The WAL only makes PostgreSQL crash-safe if each log record reaches the disk before the page it describes. With fsync off, PostgreSQL stops making sure of that, so the power cut left pages and log on disk in any order: some changes on pages with no log behind them, some log never written. That's corruption, not just a few lost transactions, and the manual warns it can be unrecoverable. Now: don't trust the damaged files. Restore the last good backup and replay archived WAL up to the cut if you have it, which is point-in-time recovery, or rebuild from the booking source. Next time leave fsync on. If month-end commits are too slow, set synchronous_commit = off for that work, which can lose the last few commits in a crash but never corrupts the database, or give the WAL a faster disk.

next: Next, The Copy That Lags: twin town halls, and copying every change to a second database that is always a little behind.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 28.3 Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) (a standard method for ensuring data integrity; changes to data files written only after WAL records describing them are flushed to permanent storage; roll-forward recovery, also known as REDO; only the WAL file needs flushing to commit; written sequentially; one fsync may commit many transactions)

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 28.6 WAL Internals (the Log Sequence Number, a byte offset into the WAL increasing monotonically with each new record; pg_control and the checkpoint record at the start of recovery; disk drives that falsely report a successful write)
PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 66.6 Database Page Layout (PageHeaderData: pd_lsn, the next byte after the last byte of the WAL record for the last change to this page)

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 28.5 WAL Configuration (checkpoints: all dirty data pages flushed and a checkpoint record written; recovery starts from the latest checkpoint record's redo record; checkpoint_timeout 5 minutes and max_wal_size 1 GB by default; full_page_writes logs the entire page on its first change after a checkpoint)

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 19.5 Write Ahead Log settings (fsync: off can result in unrecoverable data corruption in the event of a power failure or system crash; synchronous_commit, on by default, off risks losing recent allegedly-committed transactions but not database inconsistency, maximum delay three times wal_writer_delay; wal_writer_delay default 200ms)

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 28.4 Asynchronous Commit (the risk is data loss, not data corruption; transactions replayed in commit order; fsync = off could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state)

MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, 17.6.5 Redo Log (a disk-based data structure used during crash recovery to correct data written by incomplete transactions; an ever-increasing LSN; replayed during initialization and before connections are accepted)

MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, 17.14 InnoDB Startup Options and System Variables: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit (default 1, required for full ACID compliance; 0 and 2 flush once per second, and transactions whose logs have not been flushed can be lost in a crash)

C. Mohan (with D. Haderle, B. Lindsay, H. Pirahesh and P. Schwarz), ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging, ACM Transactions on Database Systems, March 1992; talk abstract at Brandeis University (a log sequence number in each page; repeating history)

UpGuard: ISO 27001 Control 8.13, Information Backup (a summary of the control, not the standard's own text: maintain backup copies of information, software and system images, tested regularly against a documented backup policy)
